passage:
Irawati's phone buzzed for the fourth time before lunch: an unknown number, the loan app's recovery team. Her stomach tightened. "Pay today or we will message your contacts," said the latest voicemail.

In the office pantry she whispered to her colleague Asif, "I keep thinking of taking a loan from a different app to clear this one."

"Don't," Asif said. "That's how it stacks up." He suggested she save every call log and voicemail, note the times, and go to her bank about a repayment plan. "And threats like that are harassment, Irawati. It can be reported."

She opened a notes file and began listing the date, the number and what was said. Her hands slowed. She would ask the bank for an appointment first thing tomorrow.

qa.q: What did the latest voicemail threaten?
qa.a: It said that if she did not pay today they would message her contacts.

qa.q: What was Irawati tempted to do, and what does it show about her state?
qa.a: She was tempted to take a loan from a different app to clear this one, which shows how anxious and cornered she felt.
Save the call logs and voicemails, note dates and times, talk to the bank about a repayment plan, and report the harassment.

qa.q: How does Asif see the idea of a second loan?
qa.a: Asif sees it as a trap, since that is how debt stacks up.

grounding: Calls from a loan app's recovery team make Irawati anxious; a colleague steers her to keep records, talk to the bank and avoid a new loan.

passage:
In Anjali's small town near Sagar, everyone knew everyone. So when the loan app's recovery agents started calling nine times a day, threatening to message her "whole contact list", her hands shook every time the phone buzzed. She'd borrowed a small amount for her mother's medicines. The interest had become monstrous.
Another app offered her a quick loan to pay the first. She almost pressed accept.
Her brother Karthik found her staring at it. "Don't. That's how people drown."
They sat together on the verandah. Karthik helped her record every call and screenshot every threat. He said the threats were harassment, not a normal part of lending, and it wasn't her fault.
The next day they went to the bank branch in town where Anjali had her salary account, and asked about a small personal loan with a proper schedule to close the app loan. The officer explained the options slowly. Anjali also filed a complaint about the harassment at the police station, with her screenshots.

qa.q: How many times a day did the recovery agents call?
What was Anjali feeling when the phone buzzed?
qa.a: She felt anxious and frightened, her hands shaking, afraid the agents would message her whole contact list.

qa.q: What did Anjali and Karthik do instead of taking another app loan?
qa.a: They recorded the calls and threats, asked her bank about a proper loan to close the app loan, and filed a harassment complaint at the police station.

qa.q: How might Karthik see the second app's offer?
qa.a: Karthik sees it as a trap that would deepen the debt, and feels protective of his sister.

grounding: Loan-app recovery calls make the protagonist anxious; she keeps records, talks to her bank about proper options, and avoids borrowing from a new app to repay the old.

passage:
Emeka had borrowed from a quick-loan app in Lagos to fix his motorbike. Three weeks later, the app's agents were calling his phone twenty times a day, shouting, sending messages that called him a "thief". One of them said they would post his photo online. He stopped sleeping.
His flatmate Daniel found him at 2 a.m., scrolling through another loan app. "What are you doing?"
"Borrowing to pay the first one. Just to make it stop."
Daniel sat down. "That'll make it worse, not stop."
Emeka's shoulders sagged. He was so tired.
The next morning, with Daniel beside him, he screenshotted every threatening message, saved the call logs, and went to his bank to ask whether they could offer a proper repayment plan. He also reported the app's harassment to the consumer protection agency. The threats didn't stop at once. But Emeka was no longer fighting them alone at 2 a.m.

qa.q: How many times a day were the app's agents calling Emeka?
What was Emeka feeling when Daniel found him at 2 a.m.?
qa.a: He felt frightened and exhausted, desperate to make the threatening calls stop.

qa.q: What did Emeka do instead of borrowing from another app?
qa.a: He saved screenshots and call logs, asked his bank about a proper repayment plan, and reported the harassment to the consumer protection agency.

qa.q: How might Daniel see Emeka's plan to borrow again?
qa.a: Daniel sees it as a trap that would make things worse, and is worried enough to stay beside him the next morning.

grounding: Threatening calls from a loan app make the protagonist anxious; he keeps records, talks to his bank, reports the harassment and avoids borrowing again to repay.
